## Phase I — The advisory war and escalation (Jan 1964 – Jul 1965)

### Overview (changed)

The war that COMUSMACV inherits on 1 January 1964 is an advisory war that is being lost. Two months earlier the coup of 1 November 1963 had killed Ngo Dinh Diem and his brother Nhu, and with them went the province chiefs, the Strategic Hamlet Program and most of the administrative continuity the Republic of Vietnam possessed. The Military Assistance Command, Vietnam, under General Paul D. Harkins, is a headquarters of advisers, helicopter companies and support troops; the United States has about 23,300 military personnel in the country by the end of 1964, none of them formed into combat units, and 147 die by hostile action that year¹. The fighting is done by the Army of the Republic of Vietnam, the Regional and Popular Forces, and the Civilian Irregular Defense Group camps of the US Special Forces, against a Viet Cong movement that has rebuilt itself since 1959 on the political infrastructure left from the war against France and on cadres regrouped to the North in 1954 and now returning down the Trail.

Phase I runs from January 1964 to the end of July 1965. Its shape is a double collapse and a double response. In Saigon, the state comes apart: between January 1964 and June 1965 the government changes hands by coup or forced resignation repeatedly, and the generals spend more of their energy on each other than on the countryside. In the field, the Viet Cong move from the guerrilla phase to the mobile-war phase, forming regiments and then a division in the provinces around Saigon; at Binh Gia, Ba Gia and Dong Xoai they beat the general reserve and its regiments in set-piece battles, and at Song Be the government holds a province capital only narrowly and with American firepower. In Hanoi, the Politburo decides that the moment for decisive victory has come and commits regular PAVN regiments to the South for the first time. The American response comes in two steps: from the air, beginning with the reprisal strikes of August 1964 and February 1965 and hardening in March 1965 into an opening strike on the North's whole target list and a campaign run from Saigon without zones or pauses; and on the ground, beginning with two Marine battalions sent to guard an airfield in March 1965 and ending with the President's decision of July 1965 to commit US ground forces to the war in strength.

Every one of the political constraints that will shape the war is drawn in this phase: the bar on ground operations in Laos and Cambodia and the decision to fight without calling up the reserves; in this war the restricted zones around Hanoi and Haiphong and the President's approval of targets in the North are never drawn. So is the enemy's basic answer to American firepower: the decision to close in, choose the time of battle, and keep his base areas beyond the border.

Five things in this phase are new, and all of them begin on its first day. Neither the coups in Saigon nor the summer offensive turns on any of them.

The first two belong to the Republic itself. On 1 January 1964 the junta decrees land to the tiller, confirming by name what the Viet Minh and the Front had already given, and an independent Commission Against Corruption with an American power to suspend aid behind it; the same session gives the Republic a resident rural police with a Special Branch, and province and district chiefs chosen by examination from a ranked list. Khanh's coup tests both within a month and both survive it. By the end of July 1965 about 330,000 hectares are titled, the rent stop holds in most government-held districts, and the musters have shown the RVNAF to be about 41,000 men smaller than its rolls²; about 1,100 village police posts stand in the held belt, about two-thirds of the chiefs have come from the list, and the Front has killed about 410 constables, nearly all in posts settled ahead of night security³. The reforms also give the coup-makers a new grievance and Hanoi a new reason to hurry.

The third is what this command can see. Two U-2S and four Global Hawks fly from January 1964. The coastal picket closes the trawler route within a year, and Hanoi moves its southern supply to Sihanoukville about eighteen months before it did historically. On the night of 4 August 1964 the radar shows no torpedo boats near the destroyers, Pierce Arrow is not flown, and the Southeast Asia Resolution passes on the real attack of 2 August alone.

The fourth is in the hands of the men who fight: modern carbines for the whole RVNAF and the territorials, and a belt-fed gun and a marksman in every regular squad. In the held belt a post with its Popular Forces platoon now holds about nine attacks in ten. Binh Gia, Ba Gia and Dong Xoai are still lost, because the enemy still chooses where and when to fight, but they are lost at a smaller price and no battalion of the general reserve is wiped out. The outposts that fall give the Front the same carbines.

The fifth waits on Guam: B-52Js carrying GPS-guided bombs and, from March 1964, a coordinate cell at Tan Son Nhut that measures the U-2S's imagery into targets for them. Washington refuses every request to use them over the North, and the first Arc Light strike of June 1965 flies without tankers and finds as little as history's did.

A sixth thing begins on the same first day and does not show until the second year. The decree of 1 January 1964 puts a Phung Hoang committee over the new Special Branch and orders a coordinating centre in every province and district, built on the posts and files the police decree creates; the centres are staffed by the Special Branch, the Military Security Service and the sector S2, forbidden quotas, held to warrants under the police statute, and audited by the Commission. About 100 district centres are open by the end of 1964 and all of them by the end of 1965. In the same month the Army begins to select its field advisers by board, to train them for eight months in Vietnamese and in advising, and to keep them eighteen months; the first of them reach the subsectors and battalions in October. In March 1965 the centre at Hoc Mon breaks the district committee above the hamlets the police had already cleared, and the Front learns that leaving a village no longer puts its leaders out of reach.

A seventh thing began before the first day, and it is the only one that reaches back past it. Since 1957 every new officer of the ARVN, and every new American officer, has passed a branch course after commissioning and the courses of the 2026 continuum before each promotion, so that on 1 January 1964 seven such classes, about 10,000–14,000 ARVN officers, hold most of the platoons and companies of the army⁴. The session of 1 January gives that army an Officer Selection and Promotion Board with written criteria, a rated evaluation report, central command lists for battalions and regiments, relief for cause, a path to commission for proven sergeants, and a ranked list from which generals and division commanders must be chosen, behind an American aid condition. Khanh's coup tests it in its first month. Its effect in this phase is in the companies, where the educated officers already stand, and in the first battalions the board fills; Ba Gia and Dong Xoai are still lost, because the enemy chose them and the generals planned the relief.

An eighth thing stood on the first day, and it was made of steel and copper. The Republic began the war with an industrial base a generation above its own: a steelworks, an arsenal and rebuild works at Bien Hoa, a radio plant, a battery works and a wire mill at Go Vap, placed under a Directorate of Defence Industry. For fourteen months it had more capacity than customers, until the Aid Compliance Board made the RVNAF buy a share of its ammunition bodies, batteries, wire, radios and steel from it from March 1965. Its first effects were small and real: the Popular Forces platoons beside the police posts carried their own radios from the spring of 1964, and the Front learned to attack the posts that could not call; the bridges the November floods took on the coast were back in six weeks rather than months. No battle of the phase turned on it.

A ninth thing stood in the ranks on the first day, and it was the plainest of them. Since 1957 every man who enlisted or was drafted into the ARVN, the Airborne, the Rangers and the Vietnamese Marines had passed a ten-week basic course on the 2026 American programme at Quang Trung or a division centre, and every Civil Guard and Self-Defense Corps recruit a six-week abridgement of it; every American recruit since 1957 had passed his own service's 2026 course. On 1 January 1964 about 120,000–160,000 of the Republic's regular soldiers and about 60,000–100,000 of its territorials had been trained so, and the rule that nobody joined a unit untrained was put on the muster roll as a course number the Muster Service could check⁵. It changed no battle's choice of ground in the phase. It changed how the posts' first ten minutes went at Long Huu, how many of the 1st Battalion, 7th Regiment came back from Thuan Loi, and how many wounded men in both armies were alive in the morning.

A tenth thing stood between the private and the officer, and it had been there since 1957 as well. Every NCO of the ARVN, the Airborne, the Rangers, the Vietnamese Marines, the VNAF and the VNN, and every sergeant and corporal of the Civil Guard and the Self-Defense Corps, had passed the course for his grade at the National NCO Academy at Nha Trang, a division school or a territorial centre before he could be promoted to the next, on a curriculum built on the American Army's of 2026; every American NCO had passed his own service's course for his grade under the same rule. It did not make more sergeants, and it took between 1,300 and 2,500 of the best ones to teach. It meant that the squad and the platoon, where the trained private met the educated lieutenant, were led by men schooled for the job, and that a corporal first class who had passed the leader's course could take an empty squad as a schooled man⁶.

The air war over the North is the phase's one changed constraint. On 2 March 1965 the B-52Js struck the whole of the North's target list in the crachin in a single night, and by 9 March the North had lost most of its power, its bulk fuel, its great bridges, its jet base and most of its fighters, and the cranes of Haiphong⁷. It answered by dispersing everything it could move, and Moscow and Beijing answered by rebuilding its sky faster than they had historically. Nothing that reached the South changed: the porters, the trucks and the Front's regiments noticed nothing at all.

### How the phase ends (changed)

By the end of July 1965 the advisory war is over. The decision to commit US ground forces in strength has been taken, the 173rd Airborne Brigade and the III Marine Amphibious Force are in the country, the 1st Cavalry Division (Airmobile) is preparing to sail, and Rolling Thunder is in its fifth month. On the other side, the Viet Cong have formed regiments and divisions in the provinces around Saigon and in the coastal lowlands, PAVN regular regiments are in the Central Highlands, and the summer offensive has broken ARVN battalions at Ba Gia and Dong Xoai faster than they could be rebuilt, though none of the general reserve has been wiped out. In the countryside, the Viet Cong infrastructure administers, taxes and conscripts in a large share of the hamlets, and outside the held belt the government's pacification effort has nothing like the stable administration or the local security it needs. Inside it the summer is not the historical one: about 330,000 hectares of rice land have been titled to about 270,000 families, rent is no longer paid in most of the districts the government holds, and in those districts the government's arrival no longer means the landlord's². Where the government does not hold the hamlets at night, nothing has changed except the promise.

In Saigon, the Thieu–Ky junta has just taken power after a year and a half of coups. In Washington, the war has an open-ended authority from Congress and a decision on troops announced without the reserves, without a tax increase and without a declaration. In Hanoi, the Politburo has committed itself to winning before the Americans arrive in strength and must now decide whether to fight them. It will: in October the PAVN regiments of the B3 Front will go after the camp at Plei Me, and the Ia Drang will follow. The war that Phase II inherits is a war between two armies that each believe they can outlast the other, fought over a population that neither government has secured.

About 1,100 village posts are settled, two-thirds of the chiefs have come from the list, and the infrastructure has begun to leave the villages around the posts³. The sea route to the coast is closed and the Cambodian route open, and the enemy's rear is on the U-2S's maps while his regiments under the canopy and his cadres in the hamlets are as hidden as before. The general reserve enters Phase II weakened but whole, and the Front enters it with between 10,000 and 30,000 of the Republic's carbines⁸. On Guam the B-52Js hold about 1,400 measured targets in the cell's folders and authority to strike none of them in the North.

Phung Hoang ends the phase with about 140 district centres open, every one behind a settled post, and a method that has reached above the hamlet in one district on the edge of Saigon and in a dozen in the Delta⁹. About 1,100 selected advisers are in the subsectors and battalions, speaking to their counterparts without interpreters; the rest of the field posts are still held on the old tour. The Front has begun to move its district committees out of the held belt, which costs it the villages' daily obedience and gains it the safety of the contested edge.

By the end of July 1965 the board has filled about 70 of the army's roughly 190 manoeuvre battalion commands and relieved its first nine commanders; the rest are still held by men the generals put there, and about a third of all battalions are still commanded by captains, because the army is short of majors and the career-course gate makes none faster¹⁰. The companies are led almost everywhere by the classes of 1957–63. The generals are the generals of 1963, and every one of them has learned that the board can be bargained with and cannot be ignored.

The Directorate ends the phase with its plants at about half their capacity and the domestic share four months old; about 5,000 PF radios, 6,000 hamlet radios and 600,000 dry cells have gone to the held belt, and the Front's mines in Long An have Go Vap batteries in them¹¹. Route 1 on the coast has been reopened after the worst flood in memory, and the Front has an industrial working class in Bien Hoa to organise.

The army that enters Phase II has trained every private it has enlisted for eight years, and every territorial; it has kept about 2,000–3,000 of its best sergeants at the training centres to do it, in the two years it could least spare them, and the Muster Service has caught the centres that sold the course short. The general reserve was broken at Ba Gia and Dong Xoai and came back from both with more of its men than on any course before this one; the battalions are steadier than history's by a band, though the enemy still chooses where they fight¹².

The NCO corps that enters Phase II has been schooled for its grades for eight years, regular and territorial alike, and about 1,300–2,500 of its best sergeants are teaching at Nha Trang, the division schools and the territorial centres, on top of the drill sergeants at Quang Trung⁶. The 4th Marine Battalion at Binh Gia and the 7th Airborne at Dong Xoai were broken and came back with more of their men than on either earlier course, because their sergeants took command when their officers fell. The enemy has the academy's leader's manual and has begun to teach its local forces the ARVN platoon's routine.

The combined command ends the phase as a channel, not yet a command. It survived Khanh's coup by passing every order through his office, and it learned in its first month that operational control means what the junta of the day allows. Seoul and Canberra have consented on conditions: a Korean countersignature on every order to a Korean formation, and an Australian casualty estimate sent to Canberra. The task force ends the phase about 1,100 strong, with one campaign that found nothing for two months and then broke the Can Giuoc security section from one notebook¹³. The Hoc Mon committee that STILL WATER drove out governs from Cu Chi, and the task force's III Corps task group has its name.

The North ends the phase without the fixed economy it began 1965 with. Its fuel is in drums, its power in village diesels, its bridges are pontoons by night, its fighters are in China, and four SA-2 battalions rotate among about twenty sites that the Js strike as they are built. About 300,000–400,000 of its people are already repairing and carrying full time, a year early, and the Politburo has held three divisions at home against a landing that is not coming⁷. The flow south is untouched, and the American decision of July is history's.

The enemy has the academy's leader's manual and has begun to teach its local forces the ARVN platoon's routine.
> 
> The combined command ends the phase as a channel, not yet a command. It survived Khanh's coup by passing every order through his office, and it learned in its first month that operational control means what the junta of the day allows. Seoul and Canberra have consented on conditions: a Korean countersignature on every order to a Korean formation, and an Australian casualty estimate sent to Canberra. The task force ends the phase about 1,100 strong, with one campaign that found nothing for two months and then broke the Can Giuoc security section from one notebook¹³. The Hoc Mon committee that STILL WATER drove out governs from Cu Chi, and the task force's III Corps task group has its name.

### Changed: The American escalation: Flaming Dart, the opening strike, the Marines and the July decision
*7 Feb – 28 Jul 1965 · Pleiku and Qui Nhon; North Vietnam; Da Nang; Washington · EVCP01-2*

*Initiative: both*

The six months in which the United States went from an advisory war to a war of its own are told here as one event, because each step made the next one. At 01:50 on 7 February 1965, while McGeorge Bundy was in Saigon and Kosygin in Hanoi, about 300 men of the 30th Company of the VC 409th Sapper Battalion attacked Camp Holloway and the advisers' compound at Pleiku, killing seven Americans and wounding 104 and destroying 10 aircraft. About twelve hours later 49 aircraft from the *Coral Sea* and the *Hancock* struck the barracks at Dong Hoi, the first strike of Flaming Dart; after the VC blew up the enlisted billet at Qui Nhon on 10 February and killed 23 Americans, about 160 aircraft struck Chanh Hoa and Chap Le¹⁴. Bundy's report of 7 February argued for "sustained reprisal", and the administration accepted it.

What the President approved on 13 February was not history's "measured and limited air action" south of the 19th parallel. In this war the theater's plan had been on his desk since the autumn: the Joint Chiefs' list of 94 targets of August 1964, extended by the MACV Combined Targeting Cell with the North's command centres, radars, power plants and bulk fuel, and a request that the campaign be run from Saigon, without zones around Hanoi and Haiphong and without pauses, with a buffer of 15 miles along the Chinese border and one strike on Haiphong's port. Johnson kept two things: the decision whether the bombing would happen at all, and its date. He gave the rest. Rolling Thunder opened on 2 March, history's date, with the opening strike of Operation HAMMER FALL on the whole list in place of history's 104 USAF aircraft at Xom Bang; the 19 VNAF A-1s still struck the naval base at Quang Khe that day, as they had historically¹⁵. The route packages divided the North between the services from the spring, as historically, but the targets in every package came from Tan Son Nhut, not from the President's Tuesday lunch⁷.

On 8 March Battalion Landing Team 3/9 came ashore at Da Nang and BLT 1/3 flew in from Okinawa, the nearly 5,000 men of the 9th Marine Expeditionary Brigade under Brigadier General Frederick J. Karch, to guard the air base that Rolling Thunder needed and the Bien Hoa attack had shown to be vulnerable. Their orders, that they "will not, repeat will not, engage in day-to-day actions against the Viet Cong", lasted three weeks: on 1 April the President approved their use in active combat and 18,000–20,000 more support troops, and on 6 May the brigade became the III Marine Amphibious Force¹⁶¹⁷.

On 7 June Westmoreland asked for a major reinforcement and by 22 July the President had authorized 44 battalions¹⁸. On 28 July, at a midday press conference rather than before Congress, Johnson announced that US strength would rise at once from 75,000 to 125,000, with more as requested, that monthly draft calls would rise from 17,000 to 35,000, and that the Airmobile Division would deploy; the reserves were not called and no new taxes were sought¹⁹. Westmoreland's concept behind it, to halt the losing trend in 1965, take the offensive in 1966 and then destroy the enemy's main forces and base areas, committed the United States to attrition against an enemy who controlled his losses by deciding when to fight.

The ground war's steps came on their historical dates for their historical reasons. The air war over the North did not. Its opening came on history's day and its shape was the theater's, and by the July decision the North had already lost what history spent two and a half years taking from it. Nothing in that loss changed the decision of 28 July, which was driven by the ARVN's defeats of May and June at Ba Gia and Dong Xoai and not by anything in the North⁷.

### New: Operation HAMMER FALL: the opening strike on the North
*2–9 Mar 1965 · Phuc Yen airfield, Hanoi (Bach Mai, the Citadel, Yen Phu, Duc Giang and the Paul Doumer bridge), Haiphong port and Thuong Ly, Nam Dinh, the Ham Rong bridge at Thanh Hoa, Vinh; Andersen Air Force Base, Guam; Yankee Station; Korat and Takhli, Thailand · EV013-1*

*Initiative: allied*

The plan began on 5 August 1964, the morning after the false alarm in the Gulf that this war never answered with Pierce Arrow. Major Edwin T. Sorrell's coordinate cell at Tan Son Nhut, which had measured the panhandle since March, was given the North above the 20th parallel, and Brigadier General Walter E. Pruitt of the 2nd Air Division was sent to build a MACV Combined Targeting Cell around it, with Captain Harlan J. Reese of CINCPAC's staff as his deputy for the Navy. The Joint Chiefs' study of 24 August gave them 94 targets in five categories, airfields, lines of communication, military installations, industry and the routes of armed reconnaissance. The cell added what the list held thinly: the Air Defence–Air Force Command and its operations centre at Bach Mai, the Ministry of Defence and General Staff in the Citadel, the national radio transmitters at Me Tri, the long-haul exchanges, the early-warning radars, the Yen Phu and Haiphong power plants and the transformer stations between them, and the bulk fuel at Duc Giang, Thuong Ly, Nam Dinh and Vinh. By February 1965 the U-2S had imaged every one of them under the standing condition's satellite link, and the cell held about 760 desired points of impact, each measured to a few metres⁷.

The President's order of 13 February set the day as 2 March. The crachin set the hour. On the night of 2–3 March the cloud over the Red River delta sat at about 800–1,500 feet with drizzle, and nothing but the bombers could strike (§1.1 D4 of memorandum 013). Twenty-four B-52Js of the 7th and 320th Bombardment Wings left Andersen in cells of three from 15:00 local time, flew about 2,200 nautical miles to entry points over the Gulf of Tonkin, and released from 36,000–40,000 feet between 23:40 and 01:15, from up to fifteen miles out. The order of the night was fixed by what could fight back. The first two cells put 70 GBU-38s on Phuc Yen's runway intersections and its 38 revetments, and destroyed or wrecked 22–26 of the 921st Fighter Regiment's 36 MiG-17Fs on the ground; eight that were on alert in the northern dispersal survived, and two of them flew to Kep at first light. The third cell struck the early-warning radars at Bach Mai, Phu Ly and Kep and the four fire-control radars the cell had located, all with GBU-38. Then the penetrators: twelve GBU-31(V)3/Bs on the Bach Mai operations centre, sixteen on the Ministry of Defence buildings in the Citadel, eight on the Me Tri transmitters. Then the fixed economy: the Yen Phu power station and Haiphong's, the transformer yards at Dong Anh and Thai Binh, the tank farms at Duc Giang and Thuong Ly, two spans of the Paul Doumer bridge over the Red River, the Ham Rong bridge at Thanh Hoa with twenty penetrators on its abutments and central pier, and the rail and road bridges at Nam Dinh, Ninh Binh and Phu Ly⁷.

The last target of the night was Haiphong's port, its one strike. At dusk the Gulf watch had counted fourteen ships in the port, among them three Soviet, two Polish and one British freighter alongside the main quay. Six Js put 120 GBU-31(V)1/Bs on the gantry and portal cranes, the transit sheds and warehouses behind the coal quay, the port's substation and the lighter basin, and none on the berths with ships alongside. The British *Dartford* lost her gangway and a lifeboat to blast; no seaman of any flag died. The port's cranes, about forty of them, were destroyed or toppled; the North's own figures, given to the Polish member of the International Control Commission, were 214 port workers killed⁷.

No J was lost or hit. The guns of the delta, about 1,500–2,100 of them, 37mm and 57mm, fired blind into cloud at aircraft five miles above their reach. The second wave flew on the first days the cloud lifted, 4 and 7 March: alpha strikes of 30–40 aircraft from the *Hancock* and the *Ranger* on Kep, Gia Lam and the guns around the struck bridges, and F-105D packages from Korat and Takhli with F-100D flak suppression on the Hanoi and Haiphong rail yards, Thai Nguyen's blast furnace under construction and the Viet Tri chemical works. The MiG-17s that had reached Kep rose on 7 March and lost two to F-8Es; the guns, now firing at aircraft under the cloud, shot down four F-105Ds, two A-4Cs and an F-8E in the week, with three pilots killed, two captured and two recovered at sea. Two more cells of Js restruck the Doumer bridge and the Haiphong power plant on 6 March on the U-2S's imagery of the 5th, the first orders of the restrike watch⁷.

By 9 March the North had lost, on this command's count checked against the U-2S, about 70–80 percent of its generating capacity, most of its bulk fuel in storage, the Doumer, Ham Rong and Nam Dinh bridges, its only jet base and most of its jet fighters, its warning net, and the cranes of its only deepwater port. Hanoi radio was off the air for nine hours and its air defence command was in the provincial switchboards for three weeks. No member of the Politburo or the Central Military Commission was killed or, as far as anyone in Saigon could tell, inconvenienced; the Ministry's buildings had been empty but for duty officers, and General Van Tien Dung's staff had worked from Hoa Lac since February. The North's civilian dead of the week, by Hanoi's count given in Geneva in April, were about 1,700; this command's own estimate was 800–1,500, most in Hanoi and Haiphong. The trucks of Group 559, the porters in the panhandle and the Front's regiments in the South noticed nothing at all⁷.

### New: Moscow, Beijing and the rebuilt sky
*10 Mar – 31 Jul 1965 · Moscow; Beijing; Hanoi; the frontier crossing at Pingxiang and Dong Dang; the airfields of Mengzi and Ningming in Yunnan and Guangxi · EV013-2*

*Initiative: enemy*

The answer to HAMMER FALL was decided in three capitals, and each decided for its own reasons. In Hanoi the Politburo under Le Duan, at its meeting of 25–27 March, ordered the North onto a war footing, the dispersal of every factory, depot and fuel store that could be moved, and a militia of the whole people for air defence and repair; and, reading the strike as the preparation for a landing, held the 308th and 312th Divisions and two regiments of the 320th in the delta and on the coast through the summer instead of preparing them for the South. In Moscow, Brezhnev and Kosygin, whose premier had left Hanoi on 10 February promising help, accelerated the air-defence package: SA-2 equipment for four battalions instead of two by July, about 1,000 advisers and technicians, MiG-21F-13s for the autumn, and diesel generators, pumps and trucks in place of the heavy plant the North had asked for in 1964. In Beijing, Mao and Zhou Enlai sent Chinese railway, engineer and anti-aircraft troops into the North from June, earlier and in larger numbers than they had historically, and placed three anti-aircraft divisions along the northeast and northwest railways, some inside the 15-mile buffer the Americans had left⁷.

<!-- initiative -->Beijing's own decision, taken for its own reasons, slowed Moscow's. In April Moscow asked for an air corridor across China for Antonov transports carrying SA-2 equipment and its crews, and for the use of two airfields in Yunnan; the Chinese leadership refused both, as it did historically, and required every Soviet shipment to cross China by rail under Chinese escort and at Chinese pace. The refusal had nothing to do with the opening strike. It came from Beijing's quarrel with Moscow over the leadership of the communist world, and from Mao's suspicion that a Soviet presence in Yunnan was a Soviet presence on China's frontier. Its effect was that the first Soviet battalions of SA-2 reached Hanoi in late April and May by train through Pingxiang, three to five weeks later than Moscow had promised and with about a fifth of their equipment held at the border for inspection. The VPAF was given what Moscow could not use: its surviving MiG-17s and their pilots were moved to Mengzi and Ningming in China to train and re-form, and from the autumn its regiments flew into the North from Chinese fields to fight and back to rest⁷.

By the end of July the North had about 2,500–3,000 guns rather than history's rising count, four SA-2 battalions in the Hanoi area rotating among about twenty prepared sites, and a fighter force that lived in China. Its fuel was in drums under the trees, its power in about 700 village diesels from the Soviet shipments, and its bridges were pontoons by night. It had begun to pay for the war in labour: perhaps 300,000–400,000 people were repairing, carrying and manning guns full time by July, a year before history's figure reached that size. Its rice imports from China were promised for the autumn, about 200,000 tons for 1966⁷.

### Changed: The air war of 1965: the Thanh Hoa Bridge, the missiles and the first Arc Light
*3 Apr – 27 Jul 1965 · Thanh Hoa (Ham Rong) and the Hanoi region, North Vietnam; Andersen Air Force Base, Guam; Ben Cat, Binh Duong Province · EVCP02-2*

*Initiative: allied*

The four months after HAMMER FALL were the months in which the North rebuilt and the cell learned how fast. The Ham Rong bridge over the Song Ma at Thanh Hoa, which history's 79-aircraft package under Lieutenant Colonel Robinson Risner hit repeatedly and failed to drop on 3 April, had been in the river since the first night of March. On 3 April Risner's wing flew instead against the ferries and the pontoon bridge the North had built a kilometre upstream, and against the guns that now ringed it; the MiG-17s of the 921st Fighter Regiment that history sent against the F-105s on 4 April had been destroyed at Phuc Yen or were in China, and Major Frank Bennett and Captain J. A. Magnusson came home that week²¹. The folder for Ham Rong, complete since the previous August, became the model for every bridge in the North: the U-2S's dawn pass found each pontoon, and a cell of Js or a package of F-105Ds struck it within a day or two. The requests of April and June for Js against the Dragon's Jaw, refused historically and in the record, were never needed⁷.

The missiles were seen coming and struck as they came. The U-2S's change detection showed the six-pointed pattern of an SA-2 site southeast of Hanoi on 22 March, its signals payload heard the first Fan Song emissions on 18 April, and by 24 July it had mapped about twenty prepared sites²². Under the provision there was no Soviet-technician rule: each site was struck by a cell of Js with GBU-38s on its revetments and van pads within 24–48 hours of its first image, and from May each occupied site the signals payload located was struck the same night. The North answered by preparing three or four sites for every battalion and moving the battalions by night, which was history's answer brought forward a year. The first SA-2 to bring down an American aircraft in this war was fired on 22 August, not 24 July, and Captain Roscoe Fobair's F-4C of the 47th Tactical Fighter Squadron was not lost; Spring High was never flown, because there was nothing in July for it to answer¹⁵. Over the five months to the end of July about 60–75 American aircraft were lost over the North, against perhaps 85–100 in history's same months²³, nearly all of them to guns at low level over the restruck bridges and yards⁷.

The first Arc Light, on 18 June, was flown by thirty B-52Js of the 7th and 320th Bombardment Wings from Andersen in place of the historical B-52Fs, to the South and back without tankers, so the collision over the sea that killed eight crewmen historically did not happen. The Soviet trawler off Guam still gave Hanoi about three hours' notice; the tanker track that had betrayed the bombers' heading was gone. Twenty-eight aircraft struck a suspected base area near Ben Cat, about 40 miles north of Saigon, with about 51 bombs each²⁴; two carried twenty GBU-31s each onto four structures the U-2S had imaged, and found four huts empty for days. The rest found what history found, little, and the press called it a sledgehammer swung at flies, now accurate to a few metres. It was the find-and-fix problem in its purest form, and the J changed none of it. Arc Light would run to August 1973 and fly about 126,615 sorties²⁵; here with 10–20 percent fewer maintenance men, no tanker bridge, and a carpet half as dense when it carried unguided bombs²⁶²⁷. By the end of July the B-52's war had two halves: over the North a bomber that had destroyed in a week what history's fighter-bombers spent years on, and over the South a bomber that found nothing under the canopy⁷.

## Phase II — The main force war (Aug 1965 – Dec 1967)

### Overview (changed)

Phase II is the American war at full stride. US military strength in Vietnam rises from about 184,000 at the end of 1965 to 385,000 at the end of 1966 and 486,000 at the end of 1967, and American deaths by hostile action from 1,369 in 1965 to 5,008 in 1966 and 9,378 in 1967¹. The strategy is Westmoreland's: US divisions and brigades, with airmobility and almost unlimited firepower, seek out and destroy the enemy's main-force regiments and base areas, while the ARVN is turned increasingly to territorial security and pacification. The measure of success becomes attrition, the "crossover point" at which the enemy loses men faster than he can replace them through recruitment in the South and infiltration from the North. The instrument of measurement becomes the body count, which inflates at every level of reporting and never once establishes that the crossover has been reached.

The shape of the phase is a series of large operations that win their battles and do not change the war. At the Ia Drang in November 1965 the 1st Cavalry Division meets PAVN regulars in the Central Highlands and both sides draw the lessons they want. In 1966 the operations grow (Masher/White Wing on the Bong Son plain, Hastings below the DMZ, Attleboro in War Zone C) and in 1967 they culminate in the corps-sized sweeps of Cedar Falls and Junction City. Each kills enemy soldiers in numbers the reports exaggerate, captures rice and documents, empties villages, and is followed by the enemy's return when the Americans leave. The enemy decides when to fight; most of the large engagements begin with his attack or his ambush, and he withdraws into Cambodia, Laos and the DMZ when the cost is too high. Along the DMZ the war becomes positional: the Marines are drawn from pacification in the coastal hamlets to strongpoints at Con Thien, Gio Linh and Khe Sanh under PAVN artillery fired from the North.

Behind the main-force war, three other wars run. Rolling Thunder, run from Saigon on a restrike list without zones or pauses, grows into the largest bombing campaign since 1945 against a North that owns less to bomb each month and whose air defences, rebuilt by Moscow and Beijing, grow with it; it does not stop the flow south. In Saigon, the Thieu–Ky junta survives the Buddhist uprising of 1966, writes a constitution and wins an election in 1967 with a third of the vote. And the pacification effort, neglected while the divisions fight, is reorganized under a single American manager, CORDS, in May 1967. In Hanoi, meanwhile, the militants around Le Duan conclude that the war of attrition is not being won either, and in the second half of 1967 they plan a general offensive to break it.

In this war a fourth runs beneath the other three, and it is the one the provisions of 1964 changed most. The land programme enters the phase with about 330,000 hectares titled and leaves it with about 820,000 titled to about 640,000 families². GOLDEN SHEAF, its first clearing operation in the western Delta, shows what it can do and where it stops: at the edge of what the Regional and Popular Forces can hold after dark. The Commission survives the Buddhist crisis and the election behind the Aid Compliance Board, and in 1967 convicts its first general. With a Special Branch that owns the files, a constable in about 1,500 villages and chiefs who stay, the government's own belt is cleared of resident infrastructure before 1968 rather than after it; NIGHT LANTERN in Long An is the case. The Front answers by killing the best chiefs and moving its cadres into the towns, and the police serves Ky against the Buddhists in 1966 as it served every government before. None of this alters the main-force war, which is fought on the borders and in the Highlands where few tenant farmers live. It alters what the main-force war is fought over.

The war of the enemy's rear is now counted rather than guessed. The panhandle watch counts the Trail's trucks from December 1965; the U-2S photographs the dispersed fuel drums before the POL strikes fly; and by March 1967 MACV and the CIA agree, from the radar's count of convoys out of Kompong Speu, that Sihanoukville supplies most of the arms for III and IV Corps. The counts show the bombing raising the toll on the transit without lowering what arrives, and change no rule in Washington.

Every American and South Vietnamese infantryman carries a modern carbine, and every squad a belt-fed gun and a marksman. The Ia Drang and the Hill Fights cost fewer American lives, and no Marine on 881 South dies beside a jammed rifle. The rearmed Regional Forces are good enough to be borrowed by the corps, and the districts they leave pay for it. None of it changes who chooses the battle.

Above the Trail the B-52J is allowed against fixed crossings in the panhandle from April 1966 and cuts every bridge it can measure; the enemy answers with fords, causeways and pontoons no bomb can close, and by the autumn more is moving than before. At Con Thien in September 1967 the siege is measured every night and lifts three weeks early at a heavy price to the PAVN. It is the first siege the enemy loses badly, and Westmoreland draws a lesson from it that will cost the coastal hamlets.

Three changes of 1964 run through the phase without altering its battles. Phung Hoang's centres cover every district by the end of 1965 and break the Front's district administration in the held belt before Tet rather than after it; NIGHT LANTERN takes the Can Giuoc committee itself, not only its security chief. The method spreads by its own success into the contested belt, where it becomes the historical Phoenix, and a PRU raid at Mo Duc in February 1967 makes "the American Phoenix" a press story three years early. The American battalions arrive and leave as units for twelve-month tours, trained together and commanded for the whole of them; they fight better in the contacts the enemy grants and get no more of them, and the enemy learns to aim at the week each one changes over, as it did at Dien Ban in August 1966. And the field advisers, now chosen and trained and on eighteen-month tours, are the men who carry what the American battalions forget each year.

The officer reforms change the ARVN in this phase more than any provision before them. From the board's second season in 1965 the battalions are filled from its command list, their commanders serve eighteen months and are relieved when they fail, and by the end of 1966 about three in four of the army's battalion commanders are men a board chose, against about one in two competent commanders on the historical course¹⁰. The enemy notices within a season and does what he does against every better unit: he declines to fight it, and lays his ambush for the battalion beside it, as the 272nd Regiment does on Route 13 in May 1966. The Buddhist uprising finds the board's commanders in I Corps on neither side, and in 1967 the ranked list gives the 25th Division its first commander chosen for competence, under the aid condition, while an agent in the board's secretariat gives COSVN every list it publishes. Above the battalions nothing moves: the corps are commanded by the same men, Westmoreland's strategy turns the ARVN to pacification as it did historically, and the generals still decide where the battalions go.

A fifth war runs under the fourth, in the factories. The steelworks at Bien Hoa rolls the pickets, wire and bridge spans of the countryside, at a fifth to a tenth below its rating because the Front has learned to drop the towers of the Da Nhim line. The radio plant puts a PRC-25 in every post of the held belt from 1966, and the Front answers the radio as it answered the carbine: it attacks the posts that cannot call, and at My Phuoc Tay in March 1967 it attacks a post in order to ambush the company that answers the call. The district chiefs answer with guns instead of trucks, and their platoons stay inside their wire. In Chuong Thien the posts call and nobody comes, because the corps has borrowed the companies. And at Phu Cat in August 1967 a bad lot of shell bodies teaches the army what an arsenal is worth without honest acceptance. None of it changes who chooses the main-force battle.

Under all of it, the private soldier of both armies is trained. Every ARVN recruit of the phase passes ten weeks at Quang Trung or a division centre before he joins his battalion, every territorial six weeks at his province's centre, and every American his service's 2026 course; from 1966 the drill-sergeant corps begins to return its sergeants to the battalions as platoon sergeants⁵. The effect is the one the officer reforms found: the better unit is attacked less, and the attack that is not made leaves nothing to count. The 272nd Regiment's ambush of the Bau Bang convoy breaks on trained Regional Force soldiers who cannot be trained out of riding their trucks. At the Ia Drang the troopers keep more of their wounded alive through the night at Albany. And the enemy answers the trained soldier as he answered the rifle, by moving his war to the weapon the course does not teach: in the lowlands south of Da Nang the mine and the booby trap become the principal killers of the Marines. The devaluation of June 1966 then shows what training does not buy: a trained private whose pay no longer feeds his family goes home with his training, and some of it reaches the Front.

Between the private and the officer, the sergeant is schooled too. Every ARVN and territorial NCO of the phase has passed the course for his grade at the academy at Nha Trang, a division school or his province's centre, and every empty squad in a regular battalion can be given to a corporal first class who has passed the leader's course; every American sergeant who wants a staff sergeant's rocker passes the Basic Leader Course first, at home or at MACV's academy at Bien Hoa. The squads hold their base of fire when their officers fall, as the 7th Division's did in the rice fields of Cai Be in November 1966, and the posts of the held belt keep their listening posts out at night⁶. The enemy reads all of it from the academy's own manuals and fights the posts and the battalions that keep the routine less often.

In this war the northern campaign is the theater's own, and so is its verdict. The restrike watch keeps the Red River crossings at Hanoi closed to rail more days than not, at the cost of about 2,000 men a night and a Chinese engineer regiment, and the cell's count of targets destroyed falls from about 140 a month to about 35 as the North stops owning anything worth a GBU-31⁷. There is no Christmas pause and no POL strike in June 1966, because there is no pause to offer and no bulk fuel left. The Chinese guns on the northeast railway take an American pilot inside the buffer in May 1966, and the President keeps the buffer at 15 miles.

> Phase II is the American war at full stride. US military strength in Vietnam rises from about 184,000 at the end of 1965 to 385,000 at the end of 1966 and 486,000 at the end of 1967, and American deaths by hostile action from 1,369 in 1965 to 5,008 in 1966 and 9,378 in 1967¹. The strategy is Westmoreland's: US divisions and brigades, with airmobility and almost unlimited firepower, seek out and destroy the enemy's main-force regiments and base areas, while the ARVN is turned increasingly to territorial security and pacification. The measure of success becomes attrition, the "crossover point" at which the enemy loses men faster than he can replace them through recruitment in the South and infiltration from the North. The instrument of measurement becomes the body count, which inflates at every level of reporting and never once establishes that the crossover has been reached.
> 
> The shape of the phase is a series of large operations that win their battles and do not change the war. At the Ia Drang in November 1965 the 1st Cavalry Division meets PAVN regulars in the Central Highlands and both sides draw the lessons they want. In 1966 the operations grow (Masher/White Wing on the Bong Son plain, Hastings below the DMZ, Attleboro in War Zone C) and in 1967 they culminate in the corps-sized sweeps of Cedar Falls and Junction City. Each kills enemy soldiers in numbers the reports exaggerate, captures rice and documents, empties villages, and is followed by the enemy's return when the Americans leave. The enemy decides when to fight; most of the large engagements begin with his attack or his ambush, and he withdraws into Cambodia, Laos and the DMZ when the cost is too high. Along the DMZ the war becomes positional: the Marines are drawn from pacification in the coastal hamlets to strongpoints at Con Thien, Gio Linh and Khe Sanh under PAVN artillery fired from the North.
> 
> Behind the main-force war, three other wars run. Rolling Thunder grows into the largest bombing campaign since 1945 against a North whose air defences grow with it, and does not stop the flow south. In Saigon, the Thieu–Ky junta survives the Buddhist uprising of 1966, writes a constitution and wins an election in 1967 with a third of the vote. And the pacification effort, neglected while the divisions fight, is reorganized under a single American manager, CORDS, in May 1967. In Hanoi, meanwhile, the militants around Le Duan conclude that the war of attrition is not being won either, and in the second half of 1967 they plan a general offensive to break it.
> 
> In this war a fourth runs beneath the other three, and it is the one the provisions of 1964 changed most. The land programme enters the phase with about 330,000 hectares titled and leaves it with about 820,000 titled to about 640,000 families². GOLDEN SHEAF, its first clearing operation in the western Delta, shows what it can do and where it stops: at the edge of what the Regional and Popular Forces can hold after dark. The Commission survives the Buddhist crisis and the election behind the Aid Compliance Board, and in 1967 convicts its first general. With a Special Branch that owns the files, a constable in about 1,500 villages and chiefs who stay, the government's own belt is cleared of resident infrastructure before 1968 rather than after it; NIGHT LANTERN in Long An is the case. The Front answers by killing the best chiefs and moving its cadres into the towns, and the police serves Ky against the Buddhists in 1966 as it served every government before. None of this alters the main-force war, which is fought on the borders and in the Highlands where few tenant farmers live. It alters what the main-force war is fought over.
> 
> The war of the enemy's rear is now counted rather than guessed. The panhandle watch counts the Trail's trucks from December 1965; the U-2S photographs the dispersed fuel drums before the POL strikes fly; and by March 1967 MACV and the CIA agree, from the radar's count of convoys out of Kompong Speu, that Sihanoukville supplies most of the arms for III and IV Corps. The counts show the bombing raising the toll on the transit without lowering what arrives, and change no rule in Washington.
> 
> Every American and South Vietnamese infantryman carries a modern carbine, and every squad a belt-fed gun and a marksman. The Ia Drang and the Hill Fights cost fewer American lives, and no Marine on 881 South dies beside a jammed rifle. The rearmed Regional Forces are good enough to be borrowed by the corps, and the districts they leave pay for it. None of it changes who chooses the battle.
> 
> Above the Trail the B-52J is allowed against fixed crossings in the panhandle from April 1966 and cuts every bridge it can measure; the enemy answers with fords, causeways and pontoons no bomb can close, and by the autumn more is moving than before. At Con Thien in September 1967 the siege is measured every night and lifts three weeks early at a heavy price to the PAVN. It is the first siege the enemy loses badly, and Westmoreland draws a lesson from it that will cost the coastal hamlets.
> 
> Three changes of 1964 run through the phase without altering its battles. Phung Hoang's centres cover every district by the end of 1965 and break the Front's district administration in the held belt before Tet rather than after it; NIGHT LANTERN takes the Can Giuoc committee itself, not only its security chief. The method spreads by its own success into the contested belt, where it becomes the historical Phoenix, and a PRU raid at Mo Duc in February 1967 makes "the American Phoenix" a press story three years early. The American battalions arrive and leave as units for twelve-month tours, trained together and commanded for the whole of them; they fight better in the contacts the enemy grants and get no more of them, and the enemy learns to aim at the week each one changes over, as it did at Dien Ban in August 1966. And the field advisers, now chosen and trained and on eighteen-month tours, are the men who carry what the American battalions forget each year.
> 
> The officer reforms change the ARVN in this phase more than any provision before them. From the board's second season in 1965 the battalions are filled from its command list, their commanders serve eighteen months and are relieved when they fail, and by the end of 1966 about three in four of the army's battalion commanders are men a board chose, against about one in two competent commanders on the historical course¹⁰. The enemy notices within a season and does what he does against every better unit: he declines to fight it, and lays his ambush for the battalion beside it, as the 272nd Regiment does on Route 13 in May 1966. The Buddhist uprising finds the board's commanders in I Corps on neither side, and in 1967 the ranked list gives the 25th Division its first commander chosen for competence, under the aid condition, while an agent in the board's secretariat gives COSVN every list it publishes. Above the battalions nothing moves: the corps are commanded by the same men, Westmoreland's strategy turns the ARVN to pacification as it did historically, and the generals still decide where the battalions go.
> 
> A fifth war runs under the fourth, in the factories. The steelworks at Bien Hoa rolls the pickets, wire and bridge spans of the countryside, at a fifth to a tenth below its rating because the Front has learned to drop the towers of the Da Nhim line. The radio plant puts a PRC-25 in every post of the held belt from 1966, and the Front answers the radio as it answered the carbine: it attacks the posts that cannot call, and at My Phuoc Tay in March 1967 it attacks a post in order to ambush the company that answers the call. ### How the phase ends (changed)

At the end of 1967 the United States has about 486,000 military personnel in Vietnam and has lost 9,378 of them killed by hostile action in the year¹. Rolling Thunder has dropped about 864,000 tons on North Vietnam by the Pentagon's announcement of 31 December¹⁵, and the North's air defences have made every strike near Hanoi expensive. The Trail is carrying more than ever; truck movements rise sharply from October to December. The enemy order of battle is in dispute: MACV counts about 300,000 communist personnel, the CIA up to 430,000²⁸, and the disagreement turns on whether the guerrillas and the political infrastructure, the part of the enemy the main-force war does not touch, are counted at all.

On 21 November Westmoreland tells the National Press Club that the enemy is "unable to mount a major offensive" and that "the end begins to come into view"²⁸. The administration's progress campaign of the autumn rests on the body count, the Hamlet Evaluation System and the claim that the crossover point is near. McNamara, who has lost confidence in the war, has announced his departure for the World Bank, and Johnson's offer at San Antonio on 29 September, to stop the bombing in exchange for prompt and productive talks, has been rejected by Hanoi. In Saigon there is, for the first time since 1963, an elected government under Thieu, and in the countryside CORDS has begun to organize the territorial war, from a less low base than history's. About 820,000 hectares have been titled to about 640,000 families, rent has ended in law and largely in fact wherever the government holds the night, and the Commission has convicted a general. The infrastructure of the Front is smaller in the Delta than on the historical course, and its tax take lower, but it is intact in every hamlet the government does not hold after dark, and those hamlets are still most of the contested countryside².

In Hanoi the decision is taken. The PAVN and VC main forces have been drawn to the borders and have drawn the Americans after them; the VC's local forces and cadres in and around the cities are preparing; and the Politburo has set the Tet holiday of 1968 as the moment for the General Offensive and General Uprising. The phase ends with each side certain that the other is weaker than it is, and with the population of the South, the object of the war, still largely outside the reach of either army's strategy.

In the held belt the resident infrastructure has been driven out of most villages with settled posts by the end of 1967, and the arrest count has fallen because there is little left there to arrest³. The National Police numbers about 80,000, the chiefs have mostly held their districts for two or three years, and the Front's legal cadres are in the towns, where the police knows less.

The enemy's external supply is measured: the Trail by the panhandle watch, Sihanoukville by the count, the North's roads by the Gulf watch, and every measure says that what arrives exceeds what the South's forces need from the North²². That knowledge is honest from 1965 rather than from 1970, and it has not changed the rules, the bombing or the strategy. Its main effect on Washington has been to deliver bad news early.

The RVNAF enters 1968 with the rifles it has carried for four years and a Regional Force that the corps commanders want for their own operations, bound since 1967 by the rule that keeps it in its provinces. The American army has had no rifle crisis and no inquiry, and has lost somewhat fewer men in the first minutes of its fights; it is the same army in every other respect, fighting the same battles on the enemy's terms.

The bombers have learned two things in two years: that a bridge they can measure dies in a night and is replaced by five crossings they cannot, and that a siege they can measure becomes the enemy's worst battle. The second lesson is the one the headquarters remembers going into 1968.

Phung Hoang has a centre in every district and an audited count of about 18,000 neutralized since 1965, about one in five of them members of district or village committees, and the Front's district administration in the held belt now governs from the contested edge by courier. The word Phoenix has been a press story since March 1967. About 7,000 selected advisers hold every field post below corps; the American battalions have changed over once or twice each as units, have fought better in the contacts they were granted, and have learned at Dien Ban to keep their reliefs off the dark of the moon. The staggered six-week overlap that followed raised the peak American strength in theater by about 15,000–25,000 men, which the expansion battalions of 1967 waited for, so that the enemy's tactic against the relief was paid for in American spaces rather than American dead⁹. None of it has changed who chooses the battle.

The ARVN ends 1967 with about four in five of its battalions commanded by officers the board chose, on eighteen-month commands, with the captain-led battalion nearly gone and the thirty-day review feared and read; about a third fewer of its battalions have been rendered ineffective in 1966–67 than on the historical course, which no report shows because the enemy declined the fights that would have shown it¹⁰. The 25th Division has a commander from the list and the corps have the commanders they had. The Military Security Service has its first file on the board's officers as a political factor, and COSVN has had every list the board published.

The factories end 1967 producing what the domestic share buys, with the steelworks short of power and the arsenal short of its gunners' trust after Phu Cat. Every post of the held belt has a radio, the Front attacks those that can call about a third less often than those that cannot, and where the guns can reach the posts the first call is for fire¹¹. The posts hold themselves better than the hamlets around them.

The ARVN ends 1967 trained to the man; training alone would have left it as short of squad leaders as history's, and what filled most of the empty slots was the NCO schooling described below; its battalions have lost about a tenth to a sixth fewer men in the ambushes the enemy still lays, beyond what the rifles and the officers saved, and about one in eight fewer battalions has been broken in 1966–67 than the officer reforms alone would have left. The drill-sergeant corps has begun to return about 650–1,800 platoon sergeants a year to the battalions¹². In the lowlands of Quang Nam and Quang Ngai the mine has replaced the firefight as the enemy's way of killing Americans, and in the districts around Saigon the Front's guerrilla squads are drilled by men the Republic trained.

The ARVN ends 1967 with its squads and platoons led by schooled men: about two in three of the slots the field commissions emptied are held by corporals first class who passed the leader's course, and the squads of the 7th Division held their base of fire at Hau My when their officers fell. I judge that about one in six to one in five fewer ARVN battalions were broken in 1966–67 than the officer reforms and the basic course alone would have left, and that the posts of the Delta lost about a tenth to a fifth fewer to night attack than the radio and the trained platoon had already saved⁶. None of it shows in a return: the enemy attacked less what kept its routine. American sergeants pass the Basic Leader Course at Bien Hoa or wait for it, and the waiver of 1966 has become a ninety-day deferral.

The combined command ends 1967 with one corps area under a Vietnamese commander and three under American deputies who in practice run them, a quarterly plan the corps commanders execute at their own speed, and a two-layer plan that protects its operations and insults its Vietnamese staff. The task force has broken the Front's district government of the Saigon belt from its edge: the Hoc Mon committee and the region's finance section govern from the Ho Bo woods, and the region's collections from the posted villages are about an eighth of 1964's¹³. On the II Corps coast it has a list it abandoned and a story the Front still tells.

Over the North the phase ends with the campaign the theater asked for and the result it predicted. In October 1966 this command reported that the northern campaign was destroying everything in the North that could be destroyed and that the North's war in the South needed none of it, and the barrier began from that report. The air defence that history's gradualism let the North build under sanctuary was built instead under fire and from China: about 120 MiGs fighting from Chinese fields, and SA-2 battalions three sites to a launcher. About 40–90 fewer American aircraft were lost over the North in 1966–67 than historically, and the Stennis hearings on the restrictions were never held⁷.

Rolling Thunder has dropped about 864,000 tons on North Vietnam by the Pentagon's announcement of 31 December¹⁵, and the North's air defences have made every strike near Hanoi expensive. The Trail is carrying more than ever; truck movements rise sharply from October to December. ### New: The restrike watch on the Red River
*1 Aug 1965 – 31 Dec 1966 · The Paul Doumer, Long Bien and Chuong Duong crossings at Hanoi; the Canal des Rapides and Bac Giang bridges on the northeast railway; the ferries at Phu Ly and Ninh Binh; the MACV Combined Targeting Cell, Tan Son Nhut · EV013-3*

*Initiative: both*

This event is told at length because it shows what the provision did once the opening strike was over, and why its measure of success fell as its success grew. From August 1965 the Combined Targeting Cell ran the northern campaign on a single list of about 300 targets and a daily repair list, and the Red River crossings at Hanoi were its pattern. The Paul Doumer bridge, 1,680 metres on 19 spans, had lost two spans on 2–3 March and a third on 6 March. The North did not try to rebuild it while the restrike watch stood over it. By June the Hanoi Bridge and Road Company and the Chinese railway engineers of the 1st Railway Engineer Division had built a pontoon bridge 3 km downstream, floated by night and broken into sections along the bank by day, and a rail ferry at Chuong Duong⁷.

Pruitt's cell answered with the rhythm that became its law. The U-2S's dawn pass, read at Bien Hoa by 07:30, found each crossing in use and each repair; the cell's midday list ordered a J cell for the night or an F-105D package for the next morning; the Gulf watch and the U-2S's evening pass showed whether the trains moved. Between August 1965 and December 1966 the Red River crossings at Hanoi were struck 61 times, 28 of them by Js with GBU-31s, and were impassable to rail on about 290 of the 517 days. The pontoons were the problem the J could not solve: a 200-metre bridge of steel sections is a target only for the hours it is assembled, and the U-2S saw it at dawn after it had been taken apart. The cell learned to strike the pontoon parks on the banks with GBU-38s by day and the approaches by night, and Captain Reese's carriers took the ferries; the North learned to keep three pontoon sets for every one in the river⁷.

What the watch measured was the North spending labour to keep moving. By the autumn of 1966 about 2,000 men of the Hanoi crossings' repair and pontoon units were working the river at night, beside a Chinese railway engineer regiment, to carry about 40–60 percent of the trains the bridge had carried in February 1965. The cell's own monthly count of targets destroyed rose through the summer of 1965 to about 140 a month, and fell month by month thereafter to about 35 by December 1966, as the North stopped owning anything else worth a GBU-31. In October 1966 J-2 sent Washington, beside the cell's figures, the Gulf watch's count of the coastal traffic south of Thanh Hoa and the CIA's estimate of the North's imports: neither had fallen since the spring of 1965. General Westmoreland signed the covering note: the campaign was destroying everything in the North that could be destroyed, and the North's war in the South needed none of it⁷.

### New: Christmas without a pause
*24 Dec 1965 – 31 Jan 1966 · Hanoi and the panhandle of North Vietnam; Washington; Warsaw, Rangoon and Moscow · EV013-4*

*Initiative: allied*

The 37 days in which Rolling Thunder stood down historically, from 24 December 1965 to 30 January 1966, while the President's envoys carried a peace offensive to forty capitals, did not happen. Nor had the six-day halt of May 1965 and the MAYFLOWER message that went with it. Johnson sent the envoys anyway: Harriman to Warsaw, Belgrade and New Delhi, Goldberg to the Vatican, McGeorge Bundy's messages through the embassy in Rangoon, with the "fourteen points" of 29 December 1965⁷. Without a pause to point to, they carried words alone. Hanoi's answer of 28 January 1966 was its four points and the demand for an end to the bombing, as historically; the North had lost nothing it valued by the absence of a pause, and saw no reason to pay for one.

The North lost its season of free movement. Historically the pause let it move supplies south by day and repair the panhandle's roads and bridges in the open. In this war the restrike watch and the armed reconnaissance of Route Package 1 went on through Christmas and Tet, with about 2,800 sorties over the North in the 37 days, a third of them in the panhandle. The Gulf watch counted the trucks south of Vinh at about the level of November, not the doubling it counted in the pause of history's measure. What that cost the B-3 Front and the regiments on the DMZ in the spring of 1966 was a few hundred tons, perhaps two to three weeks of the 1966 flow, which the panhandle's labour had made up by April. The President's critics in the Senate, J. William Fulbright first among them, said in the February hearings that the peace offensive had been a pretence because the bombs had not stopped; the charge cost the administration more in the press than in votes⁷.

### New: The buffer's edge: Dong Dang and the Chinese guns
*12 May – 30 Sep 1966 · The northeast railway from Kep through Lang Son to Dong Dang; the frontier at Pingxiang, Guangxi; Washington and Warsaw · EV013-5*

*Initiative: enemy*

The northeast railway carried about a third of the North's imports from China, and the provision let the cell strike it to within 15 miles of the frontier. From the autumn of 1965 that meant the yards at Kep and Bac Giang and the bridges north of Lang Son, struck weekly by F-105Ds from Takhli and monthly by Js. Beijing answered on the railway itself. The Chinese 61st and 63rd Anti-Aircraft Artillery Divisions took over the defence of the line north of Kep from the summer of 1965, and the Chinese railway engineers repaired it⁷.

On 12 May 1966 an F-105D of the 388th Tactical Fighter Wing, struck by 57mm fire over the Lang Son bridge, ran north and its pilot, Captain James R. Ainsley, ejected about 3 miles inside the buffer and 12 miles from the frontier. He was taken by a Chinese gun crew and held at Pingxiang for eleven days before being handed to the North; Beijing published his photograph and the claim that he had been shot down over China. On 19 May a flight of F-4Cs pursuing two MiG-17s from Ningming crossed about 4 miles into Guangxi before turning back. China protested at Warsaw and in the press; the President, who held the decision whether to bomb, considered for three days whether to widen the buffer to history's 25–30 miles, and did not, because the provision allowed him no pause and Rusk judged that China would not fight for a railway in Vietnam. He ordered instead that no aircraft cross the buffer's line in pursuit, and the cell kept its strikes on the line at least 18 miles from the frontier for the rest of the year. The Chinese gun divisions claimed about 40 American aircraft in 1966; the cell's own records showed about 14 lost on the northeast line in that year⁷.

### Changed: The air war over the North and the barrier, 1966–67: the fuel that was gone, Bolo and Muscle Shoals
*29 Jun 1966 – Dec 1967 · Hanoi and Haiphong; the DMZ and the Laotian panhandle; Nakhon Phanom, Thailand · EVCP02-4*

*Initiative: allied*

Three steps of the air war against the North and its roads are told here as one event, because each was measured and none changed the war in the South. The petroleum strikes that history flew on 29 June 1966, after McNamara's request of the day before, were not flown, because there was nothing in bulk to strike: the tank farms at Duc Giang and Thuong Ly had burned on the first night of March 1965, and the U-2S had watched the North's fuel go into drums under the trees, buried tanks at the crossings and barges in the delta creeks through the summer of that year²⁹. MACV J-2 told CINCPAC in September 1965 that the North's fuel was no longer a target system, and the Gulf watch, which had counted no fall in the trucks south of Thanh Hoa since March, said the same of the bombing as a whole²². McNamara had the result a year before history gave it to him, and his doubts hardened in the winter of 1965–66 instead of the summer of 1966. The bombing went on, because the President had decided it would and because nothing in the South told him to stop. The Stennis subcommittee's hearings of August 1967, in which the Chiefs blamed history's restrictions for the campaign's failure, were never held: there were no restrictions to blame, and the campaign's failure was this command's report, not the Pentagon's secret⁷.

The MiG war was smaller and more dispersed than history's. The MiG-21s that reached the VPAF in 1966 were based at Mengzi and Ningming in China and flew into the North for a sortie at a time, landing at Noi Bai or Kep only to refuel; Phuc Yen was restruck on every repair and Kep, Kien An and Gia Lam monthly. On 2 January 1967, in **Operation Bolo**, Colonel Robin Olds's 8th Tactical Fighter Wing flew F-4Cs on an F-105 strike's routes and call signs. In history seven MiG-21s rose to them from Phuc Yen and were shot down in twelve minutes without loss; here four rose from Noi Bai, refuelled from China that morning, and three were shot down. The VPAF grew more slowly than history's, to about 120 MiGs by the end of 1967 against history's 180 by 1968, and fought from China rather than over its own fields¹⁵⁷.

The **barrier** began with the Jason study of 1966 and General Starbird's Defense Communications Planning Group of 15 September 1966; here the study began from the STEADY COUNT tracks, which showed where the trucks went under canopy and how fast traffic recovered, and from the restrike watch's proof that the North's own roads and bridges, struck without pause, did not limit what went south⁷. It reached the historical conclusion that bombing alone could not stop the flow. Johnson authorized construction on 13 January 1967; the Marines built the eastern strip and its strongpoints at Gio Linh and Con Thien under fire, and the electronic western part was named Muscle Shoals on 8 September³⁰. ADSID and ACOUSID sensors dropped by VO-67's OP-2Es were relayed by EC-121Rs to Task Force Alpha at Nakhon Phanom; here they were laid where the radar's tracks ended, at the edges of the trellised stretches of Routes 911 and 912 and the fords beyond, and Task Force Alpha took the Global Hawk's tracks by teletype from its first day²². Field testing began on 25 November 1967, at a construction cost of $1–1.7 billion and about $1 billion a year to run³¹. Whether it reduced what arrived is a question for later phases.
